entities.name: Seahorse
entities.fact: Male seahorses carry the fertilised eggs in a brood pouch and give birth to the young, and seahorses click by snapping bones in their skulls while feeding and courting.

entities.name: Pipefish
entities.fact: Pipefish are straightened-out relatives of seahorses, and the males carry the eggs on their belly or in a brood pouch until they hatch.

entities.name: Sea dragon
entities.fact: Sea dragons are seahorse relatives found only in the coastal waters of southern Australia, where they drift among kelp and seagrass.

entities.name: Leafy sea dragon
entities.fact: The leafy sea dragon's leaf-like flaps are camouflage only; it swims with tiny transparent fins, and the male carries the eggs under his tail.

entities.name: Weedy sea dragon
entities.fact: The male weedy sea dragon carries the pink eggs stuck to the underside of his tail, and the species is the marine emblem of the Australian state of Victoria.

entities.name: Ruby sea dragon
entities.fact: The ruby sea dragon, deep red and living below the reach of most divers off Western Australia, was named as a new species only in 2015 and first filmed alive in 2016.

entities.name: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse lives only on gorgonian sea fans and matches the coral's knobbly polyps so well that it was discovered by accident in 1969 on a fan collected for a museum.

entities.name: Denise's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Denise's pygmy seahorse is about 2 centimetres long, lives on gorgonian sea fans and takes on the colour of whichever coral it settles on.

entities.name: Pontoh's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Pontoh's pygmy seahorse, described from Indonesia in 2008, is under 2 centimetres long and lives free among algae and hydroids rather than on a single sea fan.

entities.name: Japanese pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: The Japanese pygmy seahorse, nicknamed 'japapigu' or 'Japan pig', was known to local divers for years before being named as a new species in 2018.

entities.name: Big-belly seahorse
entities.fact: The big-belly seahorse of Australia and New Zealand is one of the largest seahorses, reaching about 35 centimetres, and the male's pouch swells hugely with eggs.

entities.name: Lined seahorse
entities.fact: The lined seahorse is the seahorse of the western Atlantic, found from Nova Scotia to Venezuela, including the eelgrass beds of Chesapeake Bay.

entities.name: Spotted seahorse
entities.fact: The spotted seahorse of the Indo-Pacific is one of the species most heavily traded dried for use in traditional medicine.

entities.name: Dwarf seahorse
entities.fact: The dwarf seahorse of Florida and the Gulf of Mexico is about 2.5 centimetres long and is listed by Guinness World Records as the slowest fish, moving about 1.5 metres per hour.

entities.name: Slender seahorse
entities.fact: The slender seahorse of the Caribbean and Brazil is a popular aquarium species that comes in yellow, orange, red and black.

entities.name: Long-snouted seahorse
entities.fact: The long-snouted seahorse lives in seagrass meadows from the British Isles to the Mediterranean and Black Sea, and often grows a mane of skin filaments.

entities.name: Short-snouted seahorse
entities.fact: The short-snouted seahorse is one of two seahorse species native to British waters and has even been found in the Thames estuary.

entities.name: Pacific seahorse
entities.fact: The Pacific seahorse is the only seahorse in the eastern Pacific, ranging from California to Peru and the Galápagos Islands.

entities.name: Thorny seahorse
entities.fact: The thorny seahorse is covered in sharp spines and is found across the Indo-Pacific from the Red Sea to Hawaii.

entities.name: Tiger tail seahorse
entities.fact: The tiger tail seahorse of South-East Asia is named for the dark bands on its tail and was once the mainstay of the Philippine seahorse trade.

entities.name: White's seahorse
entities.fact: White's seahorse, or Sydney seahorse, lives in New South Wales estuaries and clings to the shark nets of Sydney's swimming enclosures.

entities.name: Knysna seahorse
entities.fact: The Knysna seahorse lives only in a few estuaries on South Africa's southern coast and is listed as endangered.

entities.name: Zebra seahorse
entities.fact: The zebra seahorse, striped black and white, is known only from the waters of northern Australia.

entities.name: Hedgehog seahorse
entities.fact: The hedgehog seahorse is a spiny Indo-Pacific species that lives on sandy and muddy bottoms, often beside sponges, and is caught in trawls.

entities.name: Greater pipefish
entities.fact: The greater pipefish of European coasts grows to about 45 centimetres, and the male broods the eggs in a pouch under his tail.

entities.name: Snake pipefish
entities.fact: The snake pipefish of the north-east Atlantic has almost no tail fin, and its numbers exploded across the North Sea in the mid-2000s.

entities.name: Bay pipefish
entities.fact: The bay pipefish hides upright among eelgrass blades along North America's Pacific coast, from Alaska to Baja California.

entities.name: Northern pipefish
entities.fact: The northern pipefish lives in eelgrass beds along the western Atlantic coast, often alongside the lined seahorse.

entities.name: Alligator pipefish
entities.fact: The alligator pipefish drifts among seagrass and floating weed in the Indo-Pacific and has a prehensile tail with no tail fin at all.

entities.name: Banded pipefish
entities.fact: The banded pipefish has red and white rings and a paddle-shaped tail, and pairs of them work as cleaner fish on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Ornate ghost pipefish
entities.fact: In ornate ghost pipefish it is the female, not the male, that broods the eggs, in a pouch formed by her enlarged pelvic fins.

entities.name: Pufferfish
entities.fact: Pufferfish inflate by gulping water into a highly elastic stomach, and many carry tetrodotoxin, a poison far more potent than cyanide.

entities.name: Porcupinefish
entities.fact: Porcupinefish are puffers whose scales have become long spines that stand straight out when the fish inflates.

entities.name: Boxfish
entities.fact: A boxfish's body is encased in a rigid shell of fused bony plates, so it swims by sculling with its fins rather than bending its body.

entities.name: Triggerfish
entities.fact: A triggerfish locks its first dorsal spine upright and the second 'trigger' spine must be pressed to release it; many also drum by beating their pectoral fins against the swim bladder.

entities.name: Filefish
entities.fact: Filefish have skin so rough that it was once used as sandpaper, and a single stout spine on the head that they can lock upright.

entities.name: Longhorn cowfish
entities.fact: The longhorn cowfish is a boxfish with two horns over its eyes and can release a toxin into the water when it is stressed.

entities.name: Titan triggerfish
entities.fact: The titan triggerfish guards its nest fiercely and will charge and bite divers who swim into the cone-shaped territory above its eggs.

entities.name: Clown triggerfish
entities.fact: The clown triggerfish has large white spots on its black belly and a yellow mouth, making it one of the most recognisable reef fish.

entities.name: Picasso triggerfish
entities.fact: The Picasso triggerfish wears a pattern of blue, black and yellow stripes that looks painted on, and it grunts when caught.

entities.name: Reef triggerfish
entities.fact: The reef triggerfish is Hawaii's state fish, with the famous Hawaiian name humuhumunukunukuāpuaʻa, meaning roughly 'triggerfish with a snout like a pig'.

entities.name: Queen triggerfish
entities.fact: The queen triggerfish of the Caribbean and tropical Atlantic blows jets of water to flip sea urchins over and eat their soft undersides.

entities.name: Grey triggerfish
entities.fact: The grey triggerfish is found on both sides of the Atlantic, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Mediterranean, and is increasingly seen off Britain.

entities.name: Orange-lined triggerfish
entities.fact: The orange-lined triggerfish is dark green with curving orange lines and is notoriously aggressive, both on the reef and in aquariums.

entities.name: Redtoothed triggerfish
entities.fact: The redtoothed triggerfish is blue-black with red teeth and feeds on plankton in the water column above Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Yellowmargin triggerfish
entities.fact: The yellowmargin triggerfish digs large nest pits in sand and guards them as fiercely as its cousin the titan triggerfish.

entities.name: Tiger puffer
entities.fact: The tiger puffer is the prized Japanese fugu, which chefs must be licensed to prepare because its liver and ovaries are loaded with tetrodotoxin.

entities.name: White-spotted puffer
entities.fact: The white-spotted puffer is a common Indo-Pacific puffer with white spots on a grey body and white stripes on the belly.

entities.name: Blackspotted puffer
entities.fact: The blackspotted puffer, nicknamed the dog-faced puffer, has a grey body with black spots and a muzzle like a puppy's.

entities.name: Map puffer
entities.fact: The map puffer is named for the maze of dark lines over its body, which look like the contour lines on a map.

entities.name: Guineafowl puffer
entities.fact: The guineafowl puffer is black with tiny white spots like the bird, and some individuals are entirely golden-yellow instead.

entities.name: Northern puffer
entities.fact: The northern puffer of the US east coast is sold as 'sea squab', its flesh being far less toxic than that of tropical puffers.

entities.name: Green spotted puffer
entities.fact: The green spotted puffer lives in brackish South-East Asian estuaries and is a common, if demanding, aquarium fish.

entities.name: Pea puffer
entities.fact: The pea puffer from the rivers of south-west India is one of the smallest pufferfish, about 3 centimetres long.

entities.name: Mbu puffer
entities.fact: The mbu puffer of the Congo River is a freshwater giant that can reach about 67 centimetres long.

entities.name: Sharpnose puffer
entities.fact: The sharpnose puffer is a thumb-sized Caribbean puffer with a pointed snout and bright blue lines around its eyes.

entities.name: Saddled toby
entities.fact: The saddled toby is so poisonous that the harmless mimic filefish has evolved to copy its black saddles and colours almost exactly.

entities.name: Silver-cheeked toadfish
entities.fact: The silver-cheeked toadfish, a highly toxic puffer, spread from the Red Sea through the Suez Canal and now plagues fisheries across the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Mimic filefish
entities.fact: The mimic filefish copies the look of the poisonous saddled toby so closely that predators leave it alone, though it is not toxic itself.

entities.name: Scrawled filefish
entities.fact: The scrawled filefish has blue scribbles over an olive body that it can lighten, darken or mottle to match its surroundings.

entities.name: Harlequin filefish
entities.fact: The harlequin filefish eats only Acropora coral polyps and ends up smelling like the coral it eats, which hides it from predators that hunt by scent.

entities.name: Yellow boxfish
entities.fact: Young yellow boxfish are bright yellow cubes with black spots, and Mercedes-Benz modelled a concept car on their boxy shape in 2005.

entities.name: Spotted boxfish
entities.fact: Male spotted boxfish are blue with gold spots while females are black with white spots, so different that they were once thought to be separate species.

entities.name: Smooth trunkfish
entities.fact: The smooth trunkfish of the Caribbean blows jets of water into the sand to uncover the worms and crustaceans it eats.

entities.name: Long-spine porcupinefish
entities.fact: The long-spine porcupinefish has spines that lie flat until it inflates, when they stand straight out, and it is found in warm seas worldwide.

entities.name: Gull
entities.fact: Gulls are the ocean's opportunists, snatching fish from the surface, raiding fishing boats and stealing catches from other seabirds.

entities.name: Pelican
entities.fact: A pelican scoops fish in a throat pouch that can hold around 10 litres of water, which it drains before swallowing the catch.

entities.name: Penguin
entities.fact: Penguins fly underwater on stiff flippers, catching fish, squid and krill, and all 18 or so species live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.

entities.name: Atlantic puffin
entities.fact: Atlantic puffins can hold a dozen or more small fish crosswise in their beaks at once; the record is over 60 sand eels.

entities.name: Albatross
entities.fact: Albatrosses lock their wings open with a special shoulder tendon and can glide for hours over the ocean without a single flap.

entities.name: Northern gannet
entities.fact: Northern gannets plunge-dive from up to 30 metres, hitting the water at around 100 kilometres per hour, with air sacs under the skin to cushion the impact.

entities.name: Cormorant
entities.fact: Cormorants have feathers that soak up water, which helps them dive after fish, so they stand with wings spread to dry afterwards.

entities.name: Osprey
entities.fact: The osprey hits the water feet-first and has a reversible outer toe and spiny foot pads to grip slippery fish.

entities.name: Tern
entities.fact: Terns hover over the water and then plunge head-first to seize small fish just below the surface.

entities.name: Arctic tern
entities.fact: The Arctic tern migrates from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, about 70,000 kilometres, the longest migration of any animal.

entities.name: Booby
entities.fact: Boobies are tropical plunge-divers named from the Spanish 'bobo', meaning foolish, because they were so easy for sailors to catch.

entities.name: Blue-footed booby
entities.fact: Blue-footed boobies fold their wings and plunge-dive into shoals of sardines, and the males show off their bright blue feet in a high-stepping dance.

entities.name: Frigatebird
entities.fact: Frigatebirds avoid landing on water because their feathers are not waterproof, so they snatch flying fish and squid from the surface in flight or steal from other birds.

entities.name: Emperor penguin
entities.fact: Emperor penguins are the deepest-diving birds, recorded below 500 metres and holding their breath for more than 20 minutes.

entities.name: Brown pelican
entities.fact: The brown pelican dives head-first into the sea from 10 to 20 metres up, unlike most pelicans, which fish from the surface.

entities.name: Bald eagle
entities.fact: Bald eagles snatch fish from the surface with their talons and gather by the hundred on Alaskan coasts when salmon and herring run.

entities.name: Kittiwake
entities.fact: The kittiwake is a small, truly oceanic gull that spends the winter far out at sea and nests on sheer cliff ledges.

entities.name: Common guillemot
entities.fact: Common guillemots, called murres in North America, swim down after fish to depths of over 100 metres and lay a single pointed egg on a bare cliff ledge.

entities.name: Razorbill
entities.fact: The razorbill is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk and chases fish underwater using its wings.

entities.name: Great skua
entities.fact: The great skua, nicknamed the bonxie in Shetland, catches fish itself but is better known for robbing gannets and puffins of theirs.

entities.name: Shearwater
entities.fact: Shearwaters skim the waves on stiff wings and dive after fish and squid, some chasing them tens of metres down.

entities.name: Black skimmer
entities.fact: The black skimmer flies low with its longer lower beak slicing the water, snapping shut the instant it touches a fish.

entities.name: White-tailed eagle
entities.fact: The white-tailed eagle, one of Europe's largest birds of prey, snatches fish from the sea surface and was reintroduced to Scotland in the 1970s.

entities.name: King penguin
entities.fact: King penguins dive to over 300 metres for lanternfish and take more than a year to raise a chick, the longest breeding cycle of any penguin.

entities.name: Wandering albatross
entities.fact: The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 3.5 metres, and can circle the Southern Ocean on a single foraging trip.

entities.name: Petrel
entities.fact: Petrels are tube-nosed seabirds with a keen sense of smell that pick fish, squid and krill from the water, and the giant petrels also scavenge.

entities.name: Flightless cormorant
entities.fact: The flightless cormorant of the Galápagos has stubby wings about a third the size needed for flight and dives for fish and octopus close to shore.

entities.name: Inca tern
entities.fact: The Inca tern of the Humboldt Current coast of Peru and Chile sports a dashing white moustache and snatches anchovies from the surface.

entities.name: Guanay cormorant
entities.fact: The guanay cormorant of Peru eats anchovies from the Humboldt Current, and its droppings built the guano deposits that made 19th-century fortunes.

entities.name: Steller's sea eagle
entities.fact: Steller's sea eagle, one of the heaviest eagles in the world, catches salmon and cod along the coasts of Kamchatka and winters in Hokkaido.

entities.name: Laysan albatross
entities.fact: A Laysan albatross named Wisdom, ringed on Midway Atoll in 1956, was still hatching chicks in her seventies, the oldest known wild bird.

entities.name: Common loon
entities.fact: The common loon, or great northern diver, breeds on lakes but winters on the sea, chasing fish underwater with powerful kicks of its feet.

entities.name: Sooty shearwater
entities.fact: Sooty shearwaters fly a figure-of-eight loop around the entire Pacific each year, a round trip of about 64,000 kilometres.

entities.name: Marbled murrelet
entities.fact: The marbled murrelet fishes at sea but nests on mossy branches high in old-growth conifers, sometimes far inland; its nest was not found until 1974.

entities.name: Short-tailed shearwater
entities.fact: Short-tailed shearwaters, Australia's muttonbirds, loop around the Pacific to Alaska and back each year, a journey of roughly 30,000 kilometres.

entities.name: Bar-tailed godwit
entities.fact: In 2022 a young bar-tailed godwit flew non-stop from Alaska to Tasmania, 13,560 kilometres in 11 days, the longest non-stop flight ever recorded for a bird.

entities.name: Snow petrel
entities.fact: The snow petrel is pure white, breeds farther south than almost any other bird, and has been seen at the South Pole itself.

entities.name: South polar skua
entities.fact: The south polar skua breeds on the Antarctic coast, steals penguin eggs and chicks, and has been recorded at the South Pole.

entities.name: Antarctic petrel
entities.fact: The Antarctic petrel breeds in huge colonies on inland Antarctic mountains, some about 200 kilometres from the open sea.

entities.name: Giant petrel
entities.fact: Giant petrels are the vultures of the Southern Ocean, tearing into seal and penguin carcasses, but they also catch fish, squid and krill at sea.

entities.name: Adélie penguin
entities.fact: Adélie penguins nest on ice-free Antarctic rock and build their nests from pebbles, which they also steal from their neighbours.

entities.name: Chinstrap penguin
entities.fact: Chinstrap penguins, named for the thin black line under their chins, breed in enormous colonies on the islands around Antarctica.

entities.name: Gentoo penguin
entities.fact: Gentoo penguins are the fastest-swimming penguins, reaching about 36 kilometres per hour, and have a bright orange beak.

entities.name: Macaroni penguin
entities.fact: Macaroni penguins have spiky yellow crests and are the most numerous penguins, with over 6 million breeding pairs.

entities.name: Humpback whale
entities.fact: Humpback whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, around 8,000 kilometres each way between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters.

entities.name: Sea turtle
entities.fact: Sea turtles navigate across whole oceans using the Earth's magnetic field and return to nest on the very beach where they hatched.

entities.name: Salmon
entities.fact: Salmon hatch in rivers, feed at sea for years, then leap waterfalls up to about 3 metres high on the way home to spawn, navigating by smell.

entities.name: European eel
entities.fact: European eels swim 5,000 to 10,000 kilometres from Europe's rivers to spawn in the Sargasso Sea, a journey not tracked in full until 2022.

entities.name: Grey whale
entities.fact: Grey whales travel around 16,000 to 22,000 kilometres a year between Arctic feeding grounds and the lagoons of Baja California.

entities.name: Leatherback turtle
entities.fact: Leatherback turtles have been tracked crossing the entire Pacific, more than 10,000 kilometres, from Indonesian nesting beaches to feeding grounds off California.

entities.name: Atlantic bluefin tuna
entities.fact: Atlantic bluefin tuna can cross the Atlantic in under two months and return to spawn in either the Gulf of Mexico or the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Blue whale
entities.fact: Blue whales are the largest animals ever to have lived, up to about 30 metres, and in the polar summer each one eats several tonnes of krill a day.

entities.name: Great white shark
entities.fact: Great whites can sense the tiny electric field of a hidden animal's heartbeat, breach clear of the water to catch seals, and one named Nicole swam from South Africa to Australia and back.

entities.name: Whale shark
entities.fact: The whale shark is the largest fish alive, 12 metres or more, yet it filters plankton; one named Anne was tracked over 20,000 kilometres across the Pacific from Panama.

entities.name: Green turtle
entities.fact: Green turtles that feed off Brazil swim about 2,000 kilometres across open ocean to nest on tiny Ascension Island in the mid-Atlantic.

entities.name: Loggerhead turtle
entities.fact: Loggerhead turtles nest on Mediterranean beaches in Greece, Turkey and Cyprus, and hatchlings from Japan ride currents across the entire Pacific to Mexico.

entities.name: Sperm whale
entities.fact: Male sperm whales roam from the equator to the edge of the polar ice, while females and young stay in warmer waters all year.

entities.name: Southern right whale
entities.fact: Southern right whales migrate from Antarctic feeding grounds to calve in the sheltered bays of Argentina, South Africa and Australia.

entities.name: Fin whale
entities.fact: Fin whales, the second-largest animals alive, cruise at over 30 kilometres per hour, and a resident population lives in the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Basking shark
entities.fact: Basking sharks, the second-largest fish, breach fully out of the water like great whites, and tagged ones have been tracked from New England to Brazil.

entities.name: Swordfish
entities.fact: The swordfish's flat bill can be a third of its body length and is used to slash through schools of fish; it also heats its eyes and brain to hunt in cold deep water.

entities.name: Blue marlin
entities.fact: A blue marlin tagged off Delaware was recaptured off Mauritius in the Indian Ocean, a journey of about 15,000 kilometres.

entities.name: Shortfin mako
entities.fact: Shortfin makos, the fastest sharks, can top 70 kilometres per hour, leap several metres clear of the water, and have been tracked over 10,000 kilometres.

entities.name: Tiger shark
entities.fact: Tiger sharks have serrated, can-opener teeth, and tagged ones travel over 7,000 kilometres between the Caribbean in winter and the open Atlantic in summer.

entities.name: Northern elephant seal
entities.fact: Northern elephant seals make two round trips a year between California beaches and the North Pacific, swimming over 20,000 kilometres in total.

entities.name: Blue shark
entities.fact: Blue sharks ride the Gulf Stream across the Atlantic and back, and tagged individuals have been recaptured more than 6,000 kilometres away.

entities.name: Northern fur seal
entities.fact: Northern fur seals breed on Alaska's Pribilof Islands, and the females migrate as far south as California, spending the winter entirely at sea.

entities.name: American eel
entities.fact: American eels travel from rivers as far inland as the Great Lakes to spawn in the Sargasso Sea, and one was first tracked all the way there in 2015.

entities.name: Salmon shark
entities.fact: Salmon sharks keep their bodies warm like tuna and migrate between Alaska and the subtropical Pacific off Hawaii and California.

entities.name: Spiny dogfish
entities.fact: Spiny dogfish hunt in packs, which earned them their name, and ones tagged off British Columbia have been recaptured off Japan, across the whole North Pacific.

entities.name: Pacific bluefin tuna
entities.fact: Pacific bluefin tuna spawn near Japan, and many young fish cross the Pacific to feed off California before swimming back to spawn.

entities.name: Globe skimmer dragonfly
entities.fact: The globe skimmer dragonfly crosses the Indian Ocean between India and East Africa on the monsoon winds, a multi-generation round trip of about 14,000 to 18,000 kilometres.

entities.name: Southern elephant seal
entities.fact: Southern elephant seals leave their sub-Antarctic islands on foraging trips of thousands of kilometres and dive deeper than 2,000 metres.

entities.name: Electric eel
entities.fact: The electric eel is not an eel but a knifefish of South American rivers, and its stacked electric cells deliver shocks of several hundred volts, the strongest species measured at about 860 volts.

entities.name: Shark
entities.fact: Every shark has ampullae of Lorenzini, jelly-filled pores on its snout that detect the faint electric fields of a hidden animal's muscles and heartbeat.

entities.name: Hammerhead shark
entities.fact: A hammerhead's wide head spreads its electric-sensing pores over a broad area, letting it sweep the sand like a metal detector for buried stingrays.

entities.name: Electric ray
entities.fact: Electric rays stun prey with kidney-shaped organs of modified muscle in their wings, and ancient physicians used their shocks to treat headaches and gout.

entities.name: Stingray
entities.fact: Stingrays find clams and worms buried in sand by sensing their weak electric fields with pores around the mouth and underside.

entities.name: Platypus
entities.fact: The platypus hunts with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed, finding prey entirely with about 40,000 electric sensors in its rubbery bill.

entities.name: Electric catfish
entities.fact: The electric catfish of the Nile and other African rivers can deliver shocks of about 350 volts and was depicted in ancient Egyptian tomb art.

entities.name: Manta ray
entities.fact: Manta rays, the largest rays, can span about 7 metres and sometimes leap clear of the water, crashing back with a slap; like all rays they sense electric fields.

entities.name: Sawfish
entities.fact: A sawfish's toothed snout is studded with electric-sensing pores, so it can detect prey in murky estuaries before slashing at it.

entities.name: Bull shark
entities.fact: Bull sharks hunt in murky river mouths and even far up rivers, relying on smell and their electric sense more than their eyes.

entities.name: Stargazer
entities.fact: Stargazers lie buried in sand with eyes on top of their heads, and some species deliver an electric shock from organs behind their eyes.

entities.name: Skate
entities.fact: Skates have a weak electric organ in their tails, thought to be used for signalling to each other rather than for stunning prey.

entities.name: Nurse shark
entities.fact: Nurse sharks suck prey out of crevices at night, using their barbels and electric sense to find crabs and lobsters in the dark.

entities.name: Goblin shark
entities.fact: The goblin shark's long flat snout is covered in electric-sensing pores, and its jaws shoot forward to snatch prey in the deep sea.

entities.name: Sturgeon
entities.fact: Sturgeons sense buried prey with electric-sensing pores on their snouts, and they leap clear of the water; leaping Gulf sturgeon have injured boaters on Florida's Suwannee River.

entities.name: Paddlefish
entities.fact: The American paddlefish's long paddle-shaped snout is packed with tens of thousands of electroreceptors used to detect swarms of plankton.

entities.name: Sea lamprey
entities.fact: Sea lampreys, jawless fish that latch onto other fish with a sucker mouth, can sense weak electric fields with simple receptors in their skin.

entities.name: Coelacanth
entities.fact: The coelacanth has a jelly-filled rostral organ in its snout that senses electric fields, and it was thought extinct until one was caught in 1938.

entities.name: Chimaera
entities.fact: Chimaeras, or ghost sharks, are cartilaginous deep-water relatives of sharks with electric-sensing pores on their rabbit-like heads.

entities.name: Atlantic torpedo
entities.fact: The Atlantic torpedo is the largest electric ray, reaching about 1.8 metres and delivering shocks of up to roughly 220 volts.

entities.name: Pacific electric ray
entities.fact: The Pacific electric ray hunts at night off California, enveloping fish in its disc and shocking them with up to about 45 volts.

entities.name: Spotted ratfish
entities.fact: The spotted ratfish of the North American Pacific coast is a chimaera with a venomous dorsal spine and electric-sensing pores on its snout.

entities.name: Elephant fish
entities.fact: The elephant fish of Australia and New Zealand is a chimaera that probes the seabed with its trunk-like snout, sensing the electric fields of buried shellfish.

entities.name: Lungfish
entities.fact: Lungfish, air-breathing fish of Africa, South America and Australia, carry electroreceptors in their skin like their ancient relatives the coelacanths.

entities.name: Coffin ray
entities.fact: The coffin ray, or numbfish, of Australia is a stocky electric ray that buries itself in sand and can deliver a strong shock to anyone who steps on it.

entities.name: Marbled electric ray
entities.fact: The marbled electric ray of European and Mediterranean coasts lies buried in sand by day and ambushes fish at night, stunning them with electric pulses.

entities.name: Lesser electric ray
entities.fact: The lesser electric ray of the western Atlantic is small enough to hold in two hands yet can deliver a shock of around 14 to 37 volts.

entities.name: Angel shark
entities.fact: Angel sharks lie buried in sand looking like rays, and the electric-sensing pores on their flattened heads help them ambush fish passing overhead.

entities.name: Guiana dolphin
entities.fact: The Guiana dolphin of South America's estuaries was the first whale or dolphin shown to sense electric fields, using the pits on its snout where its whiskers once grew.

entities.name: Tuna
entities.fact: Tunas never stop swimming, keeping water flowing over their gills, and leap from the water when chasing bait fish at the surface.

entities.name: Marlin
entities.fact: Marlins roam the open ocean using their spear-like bill to slash through schools of fish, leap spectacularly when hooked, and the largest exceed 4 metres.

entities.name: Flying fish
entities.fact: Flying fish burst from the water and glide on wing-like fins for up to about 200 metres to escape tuna and dolphinfish, and one was filmed gliding for 45 seconds.

entities.name: Mahi-mahi
entities.fact: Mahi-mahi, or dolphinfish, flash gold, green and blue, change colour when excited and fade to grey after death; they grow extraordinarily fast, reaching about a metre in their first year.

entities.name: Sailfish
entities.fact: The sailfish raises its tall dorsal fin to corral sardines and lights up with bright blue bars just before striking; it is widely considered the fastest fish in the sea.

entities.name: Ocean sunfish
entities.fact: The ocean sunfish, or mola, is the heaviest bony fish, weighing over 2 tonnes, and drifts the open ocean eating jellyfish.

entities.name: Yellowfin tuna
entities.fact: Yellowfin tuna often swim beneath dolphins in the eastern Pacific, which is why tuna nets once drowned dolphins by the hundreds of thousands.

entities.name: Oceanic whitetip shark
entities.fact: The oceanic whitetip shark roams the open ocean far from land and was blamed for many deaths among shipwreck survivors, including those of the USS Indianapolis.

entities.name: Wahoo
entities.fact: The wahoo is a sleek open-ocean relative of mackerel that can reach about 75 kilometres per hour and is prized by sport fishers.

entities.name: Skipjack tuna
entities.fact: Skipjack tuna is the most heavily caught tuna in the world and fills most tins of canned tuna.

entities.name: Albacore
entities.fact: Albacore is the tuna sold as 'white meat' tuna and has pectoral fins so long that they reach past its second dorsal fin.

entities.name: Bigeye tuna
entities.fact: Bigeye tuna have large eyes and warm blood that let them hunt in cold, dim water as deep as 500 metres by day.

entities.name: Striped marlin
entities.fact: Striped marlin hunt in groups, taking turns to dart into a bait ball, and their stripes flash brighter in the moments before each strike.

entities.name: Black marlin
entities.fact: Black marlin, found in the Indo-Pacific, can exceed 700 kilograms and have rigid pectoral fins that cannot fold flat against the body.

entities.name: Lanternfish
entities.fact: Lanternfish make up a huge share of all deep-sea fish by weight and rise hundreds of metres every night to feed, the largest migration on Earth.

entities.name: Opah
entities.fact: The opah, or moonfish, is the only fish known to keep its whole body warm, circulating heated blood through its gills.

entities.name: Oarfish
entities.fact: The oarfish is the longest bony fish, reaching about 8 metres, and swims upright in the open ocean, which probably inspired tales of sea serpents.

entities.name: Pilot fish
entities.fact: Pilot fish swim alongside sharks, rays and turtles in the open ocean, eating parasites and scraps while gaining protection from predators.

entities.name: Remora
entities.fact: Remoras hitch rides on sharks, whales and turtles using a suction disc on their heads that evolved from a dorsal fin.

entities.name: Silky shark
entities.fact: The silky shark is one of the most abundant open-ocean sharks and the species most often caught by tuna fleets fishing around floating objects.

entities.name: Pelagic thresher
entities.fact: The pelagic thresher stuns sardines by slapping them with its tail, which is as long as the rest of its body, a tactic first filmed in 2013.

entities.name: Lancetfish
entities.fact: The lancetfish is a deep-diving open-ocean predator up to 2 metres long with a sail-like fin, fang-like teeth and flabby, watery flesh.

entities.name: Louvar
entities.fact: The louvar is a rare open-ocean fish that looks like a tuna but is related to surgeonfish and feeds on jellyfish.

entities.name: Escolar
entities.fact: Escolar lives deep in the open ocean, and its flesh is so rich in indigestible wax that eating it can cause oily stomach upsets.

entities.name: Megamouth shark
entities.fact: The megamouth shark was unknown until one tangled in a US Navy anchor off Hawaii in 1976, and only a few hundred have been seen since.

entities.name: Bristlemouth
entities.fact: Bristlemouths, finger-length fish of the open ocean's twilight zone, are thought to be the most abundant vertebrates on Earth, numbering in the quadrillions.

entities.name: Antarctic krill
entities.fact: Antarctic krill swarm in the Southern Ocean in such numbers that their total weight, roughly 400 million tonnes, rivals that of all humans on Earth.

entities.name: Leopard seal
entities.fact: The leopard seal is the Antarctic's top seal predator, hunting penguins and other seals with a reptile-like head and massive jaws.

entities.name: Orca
entities.fact: Orcas, the largest dolphins, hunt in every ocean, and Antarctic pods wash seals off ice floes by making waves together.

entities.name: Colossal squid
entities.fact: The colossal squid of the Southern Ocean is the heaviest invertebrate, around 500 kilograms, with swivelling hooks on its tentacles and the largest eyes of any animal.

entities.name: Weddell seal
entities.fact: Weddell seals live farther south than any other mammal, chewing breathing holes in the Antarctic sea ice and diving for more than an hour at a time.

entities.name: Crabeater seal
entities.fact: Crabeater seals do not eat crabs at all; they sieve krill through intricately lobed teeth and are among the most numerous large mammals on Earth.

entities.name: Antarctic minke whale
entities.fact: The Antarctic minke whale is the smallest of the Antarctic baleen whales and was the main target of Japan's Antarctic whaling until it ended in 2019.

entities.name: Antarctic fur seal
entities.fact: Antarctic fur seals were hunted almost to extinction for their fur in the 1800s but have rebounded to millions, most of them on South Georgia.

entities.name: Ross seal
entities.fact: The Ross seal is the rarest and least-known Antarctic seal, living deep in the pack ice and singing eerie siren-like calls underwater.

entities.name: Patagonian toothfish
entities.fact: The Patagonian toothfish is sold as 'Chilean sea bass', a name invented in 1977 to make it sound appetising, and it lives to about 50 years old.

entities.name: Antarctic toothfish
entities.fact: The Antarctic toothfish grows to 2 metres in the Ross Sea, and its blood carries antifreeze proteins that stop ice crystals forming.

entities.name: Antarctic silverfish
entities.fact: The Antarctic silverfish is the key small fish of the Southern Ocean food web, eaten by penguins, seals and whales, and its eggs develop under the sea ice.

entities.name: Sea spider
entities.fact: Sea spiders are not true spiders but leggy marine arthropods, and in Antarctic waters they grow as wide as a dinner plate.

entities.name: Hourglass dolphin
entities.fact: The hourglass dolphin, black and white with an hourglass pattern, lives only in the cold waters around Antarctica and rides the bow waves of ships.

entities.name: Salp
entities.fact: Salps are barrel-shaped jelly animals that pump water through their bodies and can clone into chains metres long, blooming across the Southern Ocean.

entities.name: Crocodile icefish
entities.fact: Icefish of the Southern Ocean are the only vertebrates with no red blood cells or haemoglobin, so their blood runs clear and their hearts are oversized.

entities.name: Saltwater crocodile
entities.fact: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, up to about 6 metres, and swims between mangrove estuaries and even far out to sea.

entities.name: Manatee
entities.fact: Manatees graze on seagrass in warm estuaries and mangrove channels, surfacing to breathe every few minutes, though a resting manatee can hold its breath for 20.

entities.name: Fiddler crab
entities.fact: Male fiddler crabs wave one enormous claw to attract mates on mangrove mudflats, and their colours brighten and fade on a daily rhythm.

entities.name: Mudskipper
entities.fact: Mudskippers are fish that spend most of their time out of water on mangrove mud, breathing through their skin and leaping by flicking their tails.

entities.name: Oyster
entities.fact: Oysters cluster on mangrove roots and estuary beds, each one filtering up to about 190 litres of water a day.

entities.name: Lemon shark
entities.fact: Lemon sharks are born in shallow mangrove lagoons such as those of Bimini, where the pups stay for years among the roots, safe from bigger sharks.

entities.name: Archerfish
entities.fact: Archerfish shoot down insects with a jet of water spat from the mouth, correcting for the bending of light at the surface, and will also leap out to grab prey.

entities.name: Barramundi
entities.fact: Barramundi hatch in estuaries, grow up in rivers and swamps, and nearly all start life as males before changing into females.

entities.name: Mud crab
entities.fact: Mud crabs of Indo-Pacific mangroves have claws powerful enough to crack open shellfish, and they are the crab in Singapore's famous chilli crab.

entities.name: Blue crab
entities.fact: The blue crab, whose scientific name means 'savoury beautiful swimmer', is the famous crab of Chesapeake Bay's estuaries.

entities.name: American crocodile
entities.fact: The American crocodile lives in the mangroves and brackish estuaries of Florida, the Caribbean and Central America, and tolerates salt water well.

entities.name: Horseshoe crab
entities.fact: Horseshoe crabs come ashore in estuaries like Delaware Bay to spawn, and their blue blood is used to test medicines for bacterial contamination.

entities.name: Dugong
entities.fact: Dugongs graze seagrass meadows in sheltered bays and estuaries of the Indo-Pacific and are the only fully marine mammals that live on plants.

entities.name: Grey snapper
entities.fact: The grey snapper, or mangrove snapper, shelters among mangrove roots when young and moves out to reefs as an adult.

entities.name: Tarpon
entities.fact: Tarpon leap and somersault up to 3 metres out of the water when hooked, and as young fish in mangrove creeks they gulp air into a lung-like swim bladder.

entities.name: Heron
entities.fact: Herons stalk the shallows of estuaries and mangrove channels, striking fish with a lightning jab of their dagger-like bill.

entities.name: Snook
entities.fact: The common snook lives in the mangrove estuaries of Florida and the Gulf of Mexico and changes from male to female as it grows.

entities.name: Irrawaddy dolphin
entities.fact: The Irrawaddy dolphin has a rounded head with no beak and lives in estuaries and mangrove coasts of South and South-East Asia, as well as three large rivers.

entities.name: Bengal tiger
entities.fact: Bengal tigers of the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, swim between islands and hunt along the tidal creeks.

entities.name: Scarlet ibis
entities.fact: The scarlet ibis gets its brilliant red colour from pigments in the crabs and shrimps it probes out of mangrove mud.

entities.name: Roseate spoonbill
entities.fact: The roseate spoonbill sweeps its flat bill from side to side through estuary shallows, snapping it shut on shrimps and small fish.

entities.name: Striped bass
entities.fact: Striped bass spawn in rivers and grow up in estuaries such as Chesapeake Bay before ranging along the Atlantic coast.

entities.name: Mullet
entities.fact: Mullet feed on algae and detritus in estuaries and mangrove creeks and are famous for leaping clear of the water for no obvious reason.

entities.name: Mangrove jack
entities.fact: The mangrove jack is a snapper that lurks among mangrove roots in Australia and Asia when young and moves offshore to reefs as it matures.

entities.name: Four-eyed fish
entities.fact: The four-eyed fish of Central and South American estuaries has eyes divided in two, letting it see above and below the surface at the same time.

entities.name: Mangrove killifish
entities.fact: The mangrove killifish can live for weeks out of water inside rotting logs, flipping itself across land with its tail, and most are self-fertilising hermaphrodites.

entities.name: Crab-eating macaque
entities.fact: Crab-eating macaques forage in South-East Asian mangroves at low tide, cracking crabs and shellfish, and some use stone tools to do it.

entities.name: Mangrove monitor
entities.fact: The mangrove monitor is a lizard of Australia and the western Pacific that swims through mangrove swamps and has a salt-excreting gland in its nose.

entities.name: Fishing cat
entities.fact: The fishing cat of South Asia's wetlands and Sundarbans mangroves dives into the water to catch fish and is a strong swimmer.

entities.name: Mud lobster
entities.fact: The mud lobster of Indo-Pacific mangroves builds volcano-shaped mounds of mud over a metre high, which other mangrove animals use as homes.

entities.name: Proboscis monkey
entities.fact: The proboscis monkey lives only in Borneo's mangrove and riverside forests, swims well with partly webbed feet, and the male's huge nose amplifies its calls.

entities.name: Clownfish
entities.fact: Clownfish chirp and pop by snapping their jaws to settle rank within their anemone; every clownfish is born male, and the male guards the eggs.

entities.name: Coral
entities.fact: Corals are colonies of tiny anemone-like animals whose limestone skeletons, built up over thousands of years, form reefs like the Great Barrier Reef.

entities.name: Parrotfish
entities.fact: Parrotfish crunch coral with beak-like teeth and excrete the ground-up limestone as sand; a single large parrotfish can produce hundreds of kilograms a year.

entities.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
entities.fact: The crown-of-thorns starfish eats coral polyps, and its population explosions have destroyed large areas of the Great Barrier Reef.

entities.name: Giant clam
entities.fact: Giant clams can weigh over 200 kilograms and get much of their food from algae living in their colourful mantle, which is why they need sunlight.

entities.name: Humphead wrasse
entities.fact: The humphead wrasse can grow to about 2 metres, lives for decades, and crushes and eats toxic prey such as sea hares, boxfish and crown-of-thorns starfish.

entities.name: Whitetip reef shark
entities.fact: Whitetip reef sharks rest in caves by day, since they can pump water over their gills without swimming, and hunt in packs at night.

entities.name: Blacktip reef shark
entities.fact: Blacktip reef sharks patrol the shallows of reef flats, often with their black-tipped dorsal fins poking above the water.

entities.name: Box jellyfish
entities.fact: The Australian box jellyfish has venom that can stop a human heart in minutes, and it has 24 eyes arranged in clusters on its bell.

entities.name: Moray eel
entities.fact: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throats that lunge forward to drag prey down, and they open their mouths to breathe, not to threaten.

entities.name: Lionfish
entities.fact: Lionfish have venomous fin spines, and after being released from aquariums they have spread as an invasive species across the Caribbean and western Atlantic.

entities.name: Potato cod
entities.fact: The potato cod is a huge, placid grouper that grows to about 2 metres and greets divers at the famous Cod Hole on the Great Barrier Reef.

entities.name: Coral trout
entities.fact: The coral trout is not a trout but a grouper, red with blue spots, and is the most valuable fish caught on the Great Barrier Reef.

entities.name: Wobbegong
entities.fact: Wobbegongs are flat, carpet-patterned sharks that lie camouflaged on the reef floor with a fringe of skin lobes around the mouth.

entities.name: Blue-ringed octopus
entities.fact: The blue-ringed octopus is the size of a golf ball but carries enough tetrodotoxin to kill several adults, flashing its blue rings as a warning.

entities.name: Hawksbill turtle
entities.fact: Hawksbill turtles eat sea sponges that are toxic to most animals, and their patterned shells were the source of 'tortoiseshell'.

entities.name: Sea snake
entities.fact: Sea snakes are venomous true snakes with paddle-shaped tails, and most of them live their whole lives at sea, surfacing only to breathe.

entities.name: Irukandji jellyfish
entities.fact: The Irukandji jellyfish is barely a centimetre across, yet its sting causes agonising 'Irukandji syndrome' that can send victims to hospital.

entities.name: Dwarf minke whale
entities.fact: Dwarf minke whales gather on the northern Great Barrier Reef every winter, the only place in the world with licensed tours to swim with them.

entities.name: Flatback turtle
entities.fact: The flatback turtle nests only on Australian beaches and never leaves the continental shelf, so it is the only sea turtle without an ocean-crossing stage.

entities.name: Epaulette shark
entities.fact: The epaulette shark walks across the reef flat on its paddle-like fins and can survive for hours with almost no oxygen when trapped in tide pools.

entities.name: Tasselled wobbegong
entities.fact: The tasselled wobbegong has a fringe of branching skin lobes around its head and has been photographed swallowing a bamboo shark whole.

entities.name: Zebra shark
entities.fact: The zebra shark is striped as a pup and spotted as an adult, which is why Australians call it the leopard shark.

entities.name: Bumphead parrotfish
entities.fact: The bumphead parrotfish grows to 1.3 metres, headbutts coral to break it, and each one can eat several tonnes of coral a year.

entities.name: Nautilus
entities.fact: The chambered nautilus has survived almost unchanged for hundreds of millions of years and lives on the outer slopes of reefs, rising from the deep at night.

entities.name: Giant triton
entities.fact: The giant triton is a half-metre sea snail that hunts crown-of-thorns starfish, and its shell has been blown as a trumpet for thousands of years.

entities.name: Red bass
entities.fact: The red bass is a big reef snapper that so often carries ciguatera poison that it is a no-take species in Queensland, banned from being kept or sold.

entities.name: Sea otter
entities.fact: Sea otters keep kelp forests alive by eating the sea urchins that would otherwise mow them down, and they wrap themselves in kelp to sleep.

entities.name: Sea urchin
entities.fact: Sea urchins graze kelp with a five-toothed mouth called Aristotle's lantern, and in large numbers they can turn a kelp forest into a barren.

entities.name: California sea lion
entities.fact: California sea lions chase fish through kelp forests and are the trained 'seals' of circuses, recognisable by their small external ear flaps.

entities.name: Abalone
entities.fact: Abalone are large sea snails that clamp onto kelp-forest rocks and feed on drifting kelp, with a shell lined with iridescent mother-of-pearl.

entities.name: Harbour seal
entities.fact: Harbour seals rest on rocks beside kelp beds and hunt fish among the fronds, and they are found on coasts right across the Northern Hemisphere.

entities.name: Garibaldi
entities.fact: The garibaldi, California's state marine fish, is a bright orange damselfish of kelp forests whose males fiercely guard a nest of red algae.

entities.name: Leopard shark
entities.fact: Leopard sharks cruise California's kelp forests and shallow bays in schools and are harmless to people.

entities.name: Giant Pacific octopus
entities.fact: The giant Pacific octopus, the largest octopus, changes colour and texture to vanish against rocks, and the female guards her eggs for months without eating, then dies.

entities.name: Purple sea urchin
entities.fact: Purple sea urchins exploded in numbers off California after a sea star disease and a marine heatwave, turning vast kelp forests into barrens.

entities.name: Kelp bass
entities.fact: The kelp bass, or calico bass, hangs in the kelp fronds off southern California and is one of the region's most popular sport fish.

entities.name: Rockfish
entities.fact: Rockfish of the Pacific coast include over 100 species, many of which live for a century or more, and they hover among the kelp in schools.

entities.name: Lingcod
entities.fact: The male lingcod guards the egg mass on the kelp-forest floor through winter, and its flesh is sometimes blue-green, fading to white when cooked.

entities.name: Giant sea bass
entities.fact: The giant sea bass of California's kelp forests can exceed 2 metres and 250 kilograms, and was nearly fished out before being protected in the early 1980s.

entities.name: California sheephead
entities.fact: The California sheephead is a kelp-forest wrasse with big teeth for crushing urchins; all are born female and the largest turn into males.

entities.name: Bat ray
entities.fact: Bat rays flap through kelp beds and dig pits in the sand with their wings to uncover clams, which they crush with plate-like teeth.

entities.name: Sunflower sea star
entities.fact: The sunflower sea star has up to 24 arms, speeds along on thousands of tube feet and eats sea urchins, but a wasting disease wiped out most of them after 2013.

entities.name: Kelp greenling
entities.fact: The kelp greenling of the North Pacific hides among kelp, and its males and females look so different that they were once described as separate species.

entities.name: Kelp crab
entities.fact: The kelp crab clings to kelp stalks with hooked legs and eats the fronds, switching to animal prey in winter when the kelp dies back.

entities.name: Señorita
entities.fact: The señorita is a slim orange wrasse of California kelp beds that works as a cleaner fish and buries itself in sand to sleep at night.

entities.name: Opaleye
entities.fact: The opaleye has opal-blue eyes and is one of the few kelp-forest fish that grazes on algae and kelp itself.

entities.name: Cabezon
entities.fact: The cabezon is a big-headed, scaleless sculpin of Pacific kelp beds whose eggs are poisonous to eat; the male guards them until they hatch.

entities.name: Horn shark
entities.fact: The horn shark lives on the kelp-forest floor off California, eats urchins that stain its teeth purple, and lays spiral eggs that it wedges into rocks.

entities.name: Swell shark
entities.fact: The swell shark hides in kelp-forest crevices and gulps water to double its size when threatened, and it glows green under blue light.

entities.name: Red sea urchin
entities.fact: The red sea urchin of Pacific kelp forests can live for well over 100 years, with some thought to be close to 200 years old.

entities.name: Giant kelpfish
entities.fact: The giant kelpfish mimics a kelp blade, changing colour from green to brown or red to match the seaweed it hides among.

entities.name: Kelp rockfish
entities.fact: The kelp rockfish rests motionless among kelp fronds, often head-down, and gives birth to live young like all rockfishes.

entities.name: Blue rockfish
entities.fact: Blue rockfish school in the water column of California kelp forests and are among the fish divers see most often there.

entities.name: Norris's top snail
entities.fact: Norris's top snail crawls up giant kelp to graze, then lets go and sinks when it senses a sea star hunting it.

entities.name: Cape fur seal
entities.fact: Cape fur seals hunt in the kelp forests of South Africa's cold coast and are a favourite prey of the great white sharks of False Bay.

entities.name: Puffadder shyshark
entities.fact: The puffadder shyshark of South African kelp forests curls into a ring and covers its eyes with its tail when threatened, hence the name shyshark.

entities.name: Kelp perch
entities.fact: The kelp perch is a small surfperch of California kelp beds that picks parasites off other fish and gives birth to fully formed young.

entities.name: Pyjama shark
entities.fact: The pyjama shark, a striped catshark of South African kelp forests, starred in the film My Octopus Teacher and hunts at night.

entities.name: Phytoplankton
entities.fact: Phytoplankton are the drifting microscopic algae and bacteria that produce roughly half of the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.

entities.name: Zooplankton
entities.fact: Zooplankton are the drifting animals of the sea, from tiny copepods to jellyfish and the larvae of fish, crabs and sea stars.

entities.name: Jellyfish
entities.fact: Jellyfish are technically plankton: however big they grow, they drift with the currents rather than swimming against them.

entities.name: Plankton
entities.fact: Plankton means 'drifter' in Greek and covers every organism, from bacteria to jellyfish, that cannot swim against the current.

entities.name: Diatom
entities.fact: Diatoms are single-celled algae encased in glass-like shells of silica, and they carry out roughly a fifth of all photosynthesis on Earth.

entities.name: Copepod
entities.fact: Copepods are tiny crustaceans so numerous that they are probably the most abundant animals on the planet, and the main food of many fish larvae.

entities.name: Dinoflagellate
entities.fact: Dinoflagellates are single-celled plankton with two whip-like tails; some cause red tides and others light up the sea at night.

entities.name: Cyanobacteria
entities.fact: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria whose ancestors first filled the atmosphere with oxygen more than 2 billion years ago.

entities.name: Foraminifera
entities.fact: Foraminifera are single-celled plankton that build chalky shells, which pile up on the seabed as ooze and tell scientists about past climates.

entities.name: Radiolarian
entities.fact: Radiolarians are single-celled plankton with intricate glassy skeletons of silica, so beautiful that Ernst Haeckel drew hundreds of them in the 1800s.

entities.name: Coccolithophore
entities.fact: Coccolithophores are single-celled algae armoured with chalk discs, and their blooms can turn whole seas milky white in satellite images.

entities.name: Fish larva
entities.fact: Most sea fish start life as transparent larvae a few millimetres long, drifting in the plankton for weeks before they can swim properly.

entities.name: Crab larva
entities.fact: Crab larvae, called zoea, drift in the plankton wearing a spiky helmet and look nothing like the adults they will become.

entities.name: Sea butterfly
entities.fact: Sea butterflies are tiny swimming snails that flap wing-like lobes, and their thin shells dissolve as the ocean becomes more acidic.

entities.name: Portuguese man o' war
entities.fact: The Portuguese man o' war is not a jellyfish but a colony of specialised animals drifting under a gas-filled float, with tentacles up to 30 metres long.

entities.name: Arrow worm
entities.fact: Arrow worms are transparent, torpedo-shaped predators of the plankton that seize copepods with hooked spines around the mouth.

entities.name: Larvacean
entities.fact: Larvaceans are tadpole-shaped plankton that build a mucus 'house' around themselves to filter food, discarding it several times a day.

entities.name: Ostracod
entities.fact: Ostracods, or seed shrimps, are tiny crustaceans sealed in a hinged shell, and some species flash blue light to attract mates.

entities.name: Noctiluca
entities.fact: Noctiluca, the 'sea sparkle', is a bubble-like dinoflagellate that lights up breaking waves at night with blue bioluminescence.

entities.name: Trichodesmium
entities.fact: Trichodesmium, or sea sawdust, is a cyanobacterium that forms floating brown rafts and pulls nitrogen from the air to fertilise the tropical ocean.

entities.name: Comb jelly
entities.fact: Comb jellies move with rows of beating hair-like combs that scatter light into rainbows, and some are only a centimetre long.

entities.name: Pyrosome
entities.fact: Pyrosomes are hollow tubes of thousands of tiny cloned animals that drift in the plankton, glow when touched and can grow longer than a person.

entities.name: Sea angel
entities.fact: Sea angels are shell-less swimming sea slugs with wing-like flaps that hunt sea butterflies, their shelled cousins.

entities.name: By-the-wind sailor
entities.fact: By-the-wind sailors are coin-sized blue floats with a stiff sail that catches the wind, and storms strand them on beaches by the million.

entities.name: Emiliania huxleyi
entities.fact: Emiliania huxleyi is the most widespread coccolithophore, a chalk-plated alga whose blooms stretch for hundreds of kilometres and turn the sea turquoise.

entities.name: Calanus
entities.fact: Calanus finmarchicus is a rice-grain-sized copepod so rich in oil that it is the main food of herring, mackerel and the North Atlantic right whale.

entities.name: Phronima
entities.fact: Phronima is a plankton amphipod that hollows out a salp and lives inside the barrel, and the female raises her young inside it as she pushes it through the water.

entities.name: Marine virus
entities.fact: Marine viruses are the most numerous biological entities in the sea, around 10 million in every millilitre of seawater, and they kill about a fifth of the ocean's microbes every day.

entities.name: Pelagibacter
entities.fact: Pelagibacter ubique, from the SAR11 group, is probably the most abundant organism on Earth, a bacterium with hundreds of thousands in every millilitre of surface seawater.

entities.name: Doliolid
entities.fact: Doliolids are barrel-shaped jelly plankton that alternate between sexual and budding generations and can multiply explosively in blooms.

entities.name: Phaeocystis
entities.fact: Phaeocystis is a colony-forming alga whose spring blooms whip up thick brown foam on North Sea beaches.

entities.name: Prochlorococcus
entities.fact: Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth, yet this tiny ocean bacterium was not discovered until 1986.

entities.name: Clam
entities.fact: Clams dig into sand and mud with a muscular foot and feed through a siphon, and the ocean quahog of the North Atlantic can live for more than 500 years.

entities.name: Mussel
entities.fact: Mussels anchor themselves to rocks with tough byssus threads so strong that scientists have copied them to make underwater glues.

entities.name: Scallop
entities.fact: Scallops swim by clapping their shells together and have up to 200 tiny blue eyes along the edge of the mantle.

entities.name: Queen conch
entities.fact: The queen conch is a large Caribbean sea snail with a pink-lipped shell that is blown as a horn, and it hops along on a claw-like foot.

entities.name: Nudibranch
entities.fact: Nudibranchs are shell-less sea slugs with gills on their backs, often brilliantly coloured to warn that they have stolen stings or toxins from their prey.

entities.name: Cone snail
entities.fact: Cone snails harpoon fish with a venom-loaded tooth, and the sting of the largest species can kill a person.

entities.name: Whelk
entities.fact: Whelks are carnivorous sea snails that drill or prise open other shellfish, and the common whelk's egg masses wash up as 'sea wash balls'.

entities.name: Periwinkle
entities.fact: Periwinkles are small shore snails that graze algae on rocks between the tides and seal their shells with a lid to survive hours in the air.

entities.name: Limpet
entities.fact: Limpets clamp their cone-shaped shells onto rocks so tightly that they resist waves, and their teeth are made of the strongest biological material known.

entities.name: Cowrie
entities.fact: Cowries have glossy egg-shaped shells kept polished by the mantle that wraps over them, and money cowries were used as currency across Africa and Asia for centuries.

entities.name: Sea hare
entities.fact: Sea hares are large sea slugs named for their rabbit-like head tentacles, and they squirt purple ink when disturbed.

entities.name: Cockle
entities.fact: Cockles are heart-shaped clams with ribbed shells that live just under the sand of estuaries and can jump by flicking their foot.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck is a huge burrowing clam of the Pacific Northwest with a siphon up to a metre long, and it can live for over 150 years.

entities.name: Blue dragon
entities.fact: The blue dragon is a sea slug that floats upside down on the surface, eating Portuguese man o' war and storing their stings in its own finger-like tips.

entities.name: Spanish dancer
entities.fact: The Spanish dancer is a large red nudibranch that swims by flapping its body like a flamenco skirt and lays a red rose-shaped ribbon of eggs.

entities.name: Chiton
entities.fact: Chitons are flattened molluscs with eight overlapping shell plates, and some have hundreds of tiny eyes with lenses made of the mineral aragonite.

entities.name: Razor clam
entities.fact: Razor clams have long straight shells like an old-fashioned razor and can dig down through sand faster than a person can dig after them.

entities.name: Ocean quahog
entities.fact: The ocean quahog is a North Atlantic clam that can live over 500 years; one dredged up off Iceland in 2006, named Ming, was 507 years old.

entities.name: Murex
entities.fact: Murex are spiny sea snails whose glands gave the ancient Phoenicians the precious purple dye of Tyre, worn by emperors.

entities.name: Moon snail
entities.fact: Moon snails plough through sand on a huge foot, drilling neat round holes in clam shells, and lay their eggs in a collar of sand.

entities.name: Tusk shell
entities.fact: Tusk shells are molluscs with a tapering tube open at both ends, buried in sand, and were used as money by Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest.

entities.name: Geography cone
entities.fact: The geography cone is the deadliest cone snail, with a venom that has killed people, yet it also contains a form of insulin now being studied for diabetes treatment.

entities.name: Sea lemon
entities.fact: The sea lemon is a yellow, warty nudibranch of Atlantic and Pacific shores that eats sponges, and the Pacific species gives off a fruity, citrus-like smell.

entities.name: Slipper limpet
entities.fact: Slipper limpets live in stacks, with the males on top turning female as they age, and they have become invasive on European coasts.

entities.name: Dog whelk
entities.fact: The dog whelk drills into mussels and barnacles on rocky shores, and the colour of its shell depends on what it has been eating.

entities.name: Spanish shawl
entities.fact: The Spanish shawl is a purple nudibranch of the California coast with orange frills, which it waves while swimming to escape predators.

entities.name: Scaly-foot snail
entities.fact: The scaly-foot snail of Indian Ocean hydrothermal vents builds its shell and foot scales from iron sulphide, the only animal known to do so.

entities.name: Siamese fighting fish
entities.fact: The male Siamese fighting fish builds a nest of bubbles, wraps the female to collect the eggs in his mouth, spits them into the nest and guards it.

entities.name: Cichlid
entities.fact: Many cichlids, from African lakes to the Amazon, brood their eggs and fry in their mouths or guard them fiercely as a pair.

entities.name: Three-spined stickleback
entities.fact: The male three-spined stickleback turns red, glues a nest of plants together with a kidney secretion, and fans and guards the eggs.

entities.name: Yellowhead jawfish
entities.fact: The male yellowhead jawfish holds the eggs in his mouth for over a week, spitting them out briefly to turn them, and cannot eat until they hatch.

entities.name: Largemouth bass
entities.fact: The male largemouth bass sweeps out a nest in the shallows and guards the eggs and fry for weeks, attacking anything that comes near.

entities.name: Cardinalfish
entities.fact: Cardinalfish are small night-active reef fish, and in almost every species the male broods the eggs in his mouth, going without food.

entities.name: Tilapia
entities.fact: Many tilapia are mouthbrooders: the female scoops up her fertilised eggs and later the fry, which dash back into her mouth when danger threatens.

entities.name: Damselfish
entities.fact: Damselfish males chirp and pop by snapping their jaws to court females, then guard and fan the eggs, chasing away fish and divers many times their size.

entities.name: Goby
entities.fact: Gobies, one of the largest families of fish, lay eggs under shells or in burrows, where the male guards and fans them until they hatch.

entities.name: Lumpsucker
entities.fact: The male lumpsucker, or lumpfish, clings to a rock with a sucker on its belly and guards a pink mass of eggs through the spring tides.

entities.name: Gourami
entities.fact: Gouramis build floating nests of bubbles and the male collects and guards the eggs, and they can breathe air with a special organ.

entities.name: Discus
entities.fact: Discus parents feed their fry with a nutritious mucus secreted from their own skin, and the young graze on both parents for weeks.

entities.name: Arowana
entities.fact: The arowana leaps over a metre out of the water to snatch insects and small animals from branches, and it carries its young in its mouth.

entities.name: Bluegill
entities.fact: Male bluegill dig saucer-shaped nests in colonies and guard the eggs, while small 'sneaker' males dart in to fertilise some on the sly.

entities.name: Sergeant major
entities.fact: The sergeant major is a striped damselfish whose males turn dark blue while guarding patches of purple eggs on rocks and wrecks.

entities.name: Oyster toadfish
entities.fact: The male oyster toadfish guards the eggs in a den and calls females with a foghorn-like 'boat whistle' that can be heard from boats above.

entities.name: Wolf eel
entities.fact: Wolf eel pairs share a den for life, and both parents coil around their egg mass, guarding it for months.

entities.name: Snakehead
entities.fact: Snakehead parents guard their floating nest and escort the ball of red fry for weeks, charging at anything that approaches.

entities.name: Blenny
entities.fact: Blennies lay eggs in empty shells or holes where the male guards them, and many have tufts over their eyes.

entities.name: Plainfin midshipman
entities.fact: The male plainfin midshipman hums for hours at night to lure females to his nest under a rock, then guards the eggs; the hum has kept houseboat owners awake in California.

entities.name: Hardhead catfish
entities.fact: The male hardhead catfish, a sea catfish of the US Gulf coast, broods dozens of marble-sized eggs in his mouth for about two months, not eating.

entities.name: Bowfin
entities.fact: The male bowfin, a living fossil of North American rivers, guards the nest and then herds the ball of fry for weeks.

entities.name: Arapaima
entities.fact: Arapaima parents of the Amazon dig a nest, and the male guards the school of fry, which swim close above his head.

entities.name: Banggai cardinalfish
entities.fact: The male Banggai cardinalfish broods the eggs and then the hatched young in his mouth for weeks, so the species never has a drifting larval stage.

entities.name: Nurseryfish
entities.fact: The male nurseryfish of northern Australia and New Guinea carries the egg cluster hooked onto a bony hook on his forehead until the eggs hatch.

entities.name: Spinner dolphin
entities.fact: Spinner dolphins rest by day in sheltered bays and are named for leaping and spinning on their long axis up to seven times in one jump.

entities.name: Grey reef shark
entities.fact: Grey reef sharks patrol Red Sea and Pacific drop-offs and warn off intruders with a hunched, exaggerated swimming display before they bite.

entities.name: Stonefish
entities.fact: The stonefish is the most venomous fish known, lying disguised as a lump of rock with 13 dorsal spines that inject agonising venom.

entities.name: Bottlenose dolphin
entities.fact: Bottlenose dolphins hunt with echolocation clicks, and in the Red Sea they have been seen rubbing against corals that may act as medicine for their skin.

entities.name: Emperor angelfish
entities.fact: The emperor angelfish wears blue and yellow stripes as an adult but starts life dark blue with white rings, looking like a different fish.

entities.name: Bluespotted ribbontail ray
entities.fact: The bluespotted ribbontail ray has electric-blue spots and two venomous tail spines, and hides under table corals on Red Sea reefs.

entities.name: Crocodilefish
entities.fact: The crocodilefish lies flat on the sand with a crocodile-like head and lacy eyelids that break up the outline of its eyes.

entities.name: Giant moray
entities.fact: The giant moray grows to about 3 metres and teams up with roving coral groupers to hunt, the grouper signalling where prey is hiding.

entities.name: Sea goldie
entities.fact: Sea goldies, the orange anthias that cloud Red Sea reef walls, live in harems, and when the purple male dies the largest female turns into a male.

entities.name: Sohal surgeonfish
entities.fact: The sohal surgeonfish, with blue-and-white stripes and orange tail blades, lives only in the Red Sea and the seas around Arabia and guards its patch fiercely.

entities.name: Red Sea bannerfish
entities.fact: The Red Sea bannerfish trails a long white dorsal filament like a pennant and lives only in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

entities.name: Risso's dolphin
entities.fact: Risso's dolphins are grey dolphins covered in pale scars from squid and each other, found in deep water from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Arabian Picasso triggerfish
entities.fact: The Arabian Picasso triggerfish, with its painted-on stripes, is found only in the Red Sea and the seas around Arabia.

entities.name: Two-banded anemonefish
entities.fact: The two-banded anemonefish, or Red Sea clownfish, lives among anemones mainly in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

entities.name: Masked butterflyfish
entities.fact: The masked butterflyfish, bright yellow with a blue-black mask, lives only in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden and is seen in pairs along the reef.

entities.name: Common octopus
entities.fact: The common octopus changes its colour and even its skin texture in a fraction of a second, and about two-thirds of its 500 million neurons are in its arms.

entities.name: Sardine
entities.fact: Sardines take their name from the Mediterranean island of Sardinia, where they were once caught in abundance, and they swim in schools of millions.

entities.name: Mediterranean monk seal
entities.fact: The Mediterranean monk seal is one of the rarest seals, with fewer than 1,000 left, hiding its pups in sea caves in Greece and Turkey.

entities.name: European anchovy
entities.fact: The European anchovy supports huge fisheries in the Mediterranean and Black Sea and is cured in salt to make the anchovy fillets on pizzas.

entities.name: European sea bass
entities.fact: The European sea bass, called branzino in Italy and loup de mer in France, is one of the most widely farmed fish in the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Red mullet
entities.fact: Red mullet feel for prey with two chin barbels, and the ancient Romans paid fortunes for large ones and watched them change colour as they died.

entities.name: Striped dolphin
entities.fact: The striped dolphin is the most common dolphin in the Mediterranean, leaping and spinning in large schools far from shore.

entities.name: Common cuttlefish
entities.fact: The common cuttlefish changes colour and pattern in a fraction of a second using millions of pigment cells, and its 'bone' is sold for pet birds.

entities.name: Gilthead bream
entities.fact: The gilthead bream, with a gold bar between its eyes, is farmed across the Mediterranean and sold as orata or dorade.

entities.name: Dusky grouper
entities.fact: The dusky grouper is the Mediterranean's largest grouper, up to about 1.5 metres, and all are born female, with the biggest turning male.

entities.name: Mediterranean moray
entities.fact: The Mediterranean moray was farmed in seawater ponds by wealthy Romans, and it hunts at night, guided by smell rather than sight.

entities.name: John Dory
entities.fact: The John Dory's dark spot on each flank is known as St Peter's thumbprint, and it can shoot its jaws forward to engulf small fish.

entities.name: Red scorpionfish
entities.fact: The red scorpionfish, the rascasse, has venomous spines and is the essential fish of a true Marseille bouillabaisse.

entities.name: European spiny lobster
entities.fact: The European spiny lobster, or langouste, has no claws but long spiny antennae, and is the prized lobster of Mediterranean kitchens.

entities.name: Mauve stinger
entities.fact: The mauve stinger is a glowing purple jellyfish whose blooms close Mediterranean beaches and once wiped out a salmon farm's entire stock in Ireland.

entities.name: Noble pen shell
entities.fact: The noble pen shell is a metre-long fan mussel of Mediterranean seagrass meadows whose silky threads were once woven into 'sea silk', and a parasite has nearly wiped it out since 2016.

entities.name: Red coral
entities.fact: Mediterranean red coral is an animal whose hard red skeleton has been carved into jewellery since antiquity, and it grows only millimetres a year.

entities.name: Cuvier's beaked whale
entities.fact: Cuvier's beaked whale holds the mammal diving record, more than 2,900 metres deep and over three hours underwater, and lives in the deep Mediterranean.

entities.name: Dentex
entities.fact: The common dentex is a big-toothed Mediterranean bream prized by spearfishers and famous on Croatian and Greek menus.

entities.name: Mediterranean parrotfish
entities.fact: The Mediterranean parrotfish is the only parrotfish native to the Mediterranean, and the Romans transplanted it to the Italian coast as a delicacy.

entities.name: Salema
entities.fact: The salema, a striped Mediterranean bream, can cause vivid hallucinations lasting days when eaten, earning it the nickname 'the dreamfish'.

entities.name: Catfish
entities.fact: Catfish are named for the whisker-like barbels around their mouths, and many make squeaks and grunts by rubbing their pectoral spines in their sockets or vibrating the swim bladder.

entities.name: Frogfish
entities.fact: Frogfish 'walk' on the seabed with leg-like fins, lure prey with a rod grown from their first dorsal spine, and can change colour over days to match a sponge.

entities.name: Wolffish
entities.fact: The Atlantic wolffish has a mouthful of fangs for crushing crabs and sea urchins, and makes its own antifreeze to live in near-freezing water.

entities.name: Lion's mane jellyfish
entities.fact: The lion's mane jellyfish is the largest jellyfish, with a bell over 2 metres across and tentacles that can trail more than 30 metres.

entities.name: Goatfish
entities.fact: Goatfish dig through sand with a pair of chin barbels used like fingers, and some change from yellow to red in seconds when resting or being cleaned.

entities.name: Hogfish
entities.fact: The hogfish changes colour from white to mottled red in seconds and has light-sensing cells in its skin that let it 'see' its own colour change.

entities.name: Rabbitfish
entities.fact: Rabbitfish have small rabbit-like mouths for nibbling algae and venomous fin spines, and some have crossed into the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal.

entities.name: Squirrelfish
entities.fact: Squirrelfish are big-eyed red fish that hide in reef caves by day and grunt and chatter using muscles on their swim bladder.

entities.name: Lizardfish
entities.fact: Lizardfish sit propped on the sand on their fins with a reptile-like head and a mouthful of needle teeth, waiting to dart at passing fish.

entities.name: Hawkfish
entities.fact: Hawkfish perch on coral heads like a hawk on a branch, then swoop down on small fish and shrimps.

entities.name: Scorpionfish
entities.fact: Scorpionfish are camouflaged ambush hunters with venomous spines, named for the sting they deliver to anyone who grabs or steps on one.

entities.name: Sea mouse
entities.fact: The sea mouse is a furry-looking marine worm whose iridescent bristles were among the first natural structures found to work like optical fibres.

entities.name: Cownose ray
entities.fact: Cownose rays have a notched snout like a cow's nose, migrate in schools of thousands along the US Atlantic coast, and often leap clear of the water.

entities.name: Pelican eel
entities.fact: The pelican eel, or gulper eel, has a vast pouch-like mouth on a thin body and lives in the deep sea, where it has been filmed ballooning its head.

entities.name: Bird wrasse
entities.fact: The bird wrasse has a long curved snout like a bird's beak, used to pick small animals from coral crevices; the males are green and the females brown.

entities.name: Horse mackerel
entities.fact: Horse mackerel, or scad, are not true mackerel but jacks with a row of bony scales along the lateral line, and they school in vast numbers.

entities.name: Sea pig
entities.fact: Sea pigs are pink, plump sea cucumbers that walk on tube-foot 'legs' across the deep abyssal mud, sometimes in herds of hundreds.

entities.name: Squid
