entities.fact: Squid flash waves of colour across their skin with muscle-controlled pigment cells called chromatophores, signalling to each other and startling prey.

entities.name: Flounder
entities.fact: Flounders lie on the seabed and adjust their mottled colour to match the sand or gravel beneath them, and both eyes end up on one side of the head.

entities.name: Mimic octopus
entities.fact: The mimic octopus changes its colour, pattern and posture to impersonate lionfish, flatfish and sea snakes, and was only discovered in 1998.

entities.name: Peacock flounder
entities.fact: The peacock flounder can match a checkerboard pattern placed beneath it within seconds, relying on its eyes to judge the background.

entities.name: Humboldt squid
entities.fact: Humboldt squid flash red and white in rapid pulses while hunting in packs, earning them the Spanish name 'diablo rojo', the red devil.

entities.name: Nassau grouper
entities.fact: The Nassau grouper can switch between a barred pattern, a two-tone pattern and almost white within minutes, signalling at its spawning gatherings.

entities.name: Trumpetfish
entities.fact: The trumpetfish has a long tube-like snout for sucking in small fish, hangs vertically among sea rods, and can change colour from brown to yellow or blue.

entities.name: Broadclub cuttlefish
entities.fact: The broadclub cuttlefish hypnotises crabs by sending rippling bands of dark colour down its body, like a moving zebra pattern, before striking.

entities.name: Flamboyant cuttlefish
entities.fact: The flamboyant cuttlefish walks along the seabed on its arms and flashes waves of yellow, purple and white, a warning that its flesh is toxic.

entities.name: Caribbean reef squid
entities.fact: Caribbean reef squid talk in colour, flashing different patterns on each side of the body so they can court a mate and warn a rival at the same time.

entities.name: Day octopus
entities.fact: The day octopus hunts in daylight on Indo-Pacific reefs and changes its colour and skin texture many times an hour as it moves between backgrounds.

entities.name: Bobtail squid
entities.fact: The bobtail squid hides glowing bacteria in a light organ on its underside to erase its shadow in moonlight, and shifts its skin colour to match the sand.

entities.name: Turbot
entities.fact: The turbot, a prized flatfish of European waters, changes its spotted colouring to blend with the seabed and has tiny bony bumps instead of scales.

entities.name: Plaice
entities.fact: The plaice has orange spots on its upper side and can darken or lighten its body to match the seabed as it lies half-buried in sand.

entities.name: Longfin inshore squid
entities.fact: The longfin inshore squid changes its skin colour and pattern in milliseconds and edits its own genetic messages more than almost any other animal.

entities.name: Coconut octopus
entities.fact: The coconut octopus carries coconut shells across the sand to hide in and can change colour and texture to mimic the seabed.

entities.name: Caribbean reef octopus
entities.fact: The Caribbean reef octopus turns from mottled brown to an iridescent blue-green in an instant and hunts across the reef at night.

entities.name: Wunderpus
entities.fact: The wunderpus octopus, named in 2006, has a bold brown-and-white banded pattern it can switch on and off, and each individual's pattern is unique.

entities.name: Drum
entities.fact: Drums are named for the drumming sound they make by vibrating special muscles against their swim bladder, mostly to call mates.

entities.name: Atlantic croaker
entities.fact: The Atlantic croaker croaks by rapidly contracting muscles against its swim bladder, loudly enough to be heard when it is hauled into a boat.

entities.name: Grunt
entities.fact: Grunts are named for the sound they make by grinding their throat teeth together, amplified by the swim bladder, especially when caught.

entities.name: Piranha
entities.fact: Piranhas bark, drum and croak by vibrating their swim bladder, with different sounds for warning, confronting and snapping at rivals.

entities.name: Herring
entities.fact: Atlantic herring communicate at night by squeezing bursts of bubbles out of their anus, a discovery that won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2004.

entities.name: Red drum
entities.fact: The red drum, or redfish, drums during spawning by vibrating muscles against its swim bladder, and its blackened fillets became a 1980s craze.

entities.name: Black drum
entities.fact: Black drum make such loud, low booming calls while spawning that Florida residents have complained of a mysterious hum coming through their walls.

entities.name: Cod
entities.fact: Atlantic cod grunt and growl using drumming muscles on the swim bladder, mostly during courtship, and ship noise can drown out their calls.

entities.name: Haddock
entities.fact: Male haddock produce knocking and humming calls with drumming muscles on the swim bladder, speeding up into a continuous hum during courtship.

entities.name: Sea robin
entities.fact: Sea robins 'walk' on finger-like fin rays and grunt or croak by vibrating their swim bladder, a sound anglers hear when they lift them from the water.

entities.name: Weakfish
entities.fact: The weakfish is a drum of the US Atlantic coast that drums loudly during spawning; its name refers to its tender mouth, which tears on hooks.

entities.name: Gurnard
entities.fact: Gurnards grunt and growl by vibrating their swim bladder, which gave the fish its name from an old French word for grunting.

entities.name: Spotted seatrout
entities.fact: The spotted seatrout, a drum rather than a trout, makes staccato drumming calls at dusk in spawning season across Gulf of Mexico estuaries.

entities.name: Pollock
entities.fact: Pollock, a cod relative, produce grunts and knocks with swim-bladder muscles during spawning, much like cod and haddock.

entities.name: Silver perch
entities.fact: The silver perch is a small drum of US Atlantic estuaries that joins loud evening drumming choruses in summer, picked up by hydrophones in Chesapeake Bay.

entities.name: Corvina
entities.fact: Corvinas are drum fish of the eastern Pacific and elsewhere that croak with swim-bladder muscles, and some gather in deafening spawning choruses.

entities.name: Sculpin
entities.fact: Sculpins are spiny bottom fish of cold waters, and several species grunt and hum during territorial disputes and courtship.

entities.name: Cusk-eel
entities.fact: Cusk-eels hide in burrows by day and produce rapid drumming calls at night with swim-bladder muscles, forming mysterious evening choruses off beaches.

entities.name: Soldierfish
entities.fact: Soldierfish are red night-active reef fish that grunt, growl and click with swim-bladder muscles to defend their caves.

entities.name: Totoaba
entities.fact: The totoaba, a drum of the Gulf of California, makes booming calls with its swim bladder, the organ now smuggled as a delicacy, which has driven it close to extinction.

entities.name: Splendid toadfish
entities.fact: The splendid toadfish is found only around Cozumel, Mexico, where it hides under coral ledges and whistles to attract mates.

entities.name: Lusitanian toadfish
entities.fact: The Lusitanian toadfish of Portuguese estuaries hums and 'boat-whistles' from its nest, and larger males even sing in choruses to attract females.

entities.name: Gulf corvina
entities.fact: Gulf corvinas gather by the million in the Colorado River delta to spawn, and their chorus is loud enough to damage the hearing of nearby dolphins.

entities.name: Freshwater drum
entities.fact: The freshwater drum of North American rivers grunts with swim-bladder muscles, and its ear bones, 'lucky stones', have been found in ancient sites.

entities.name: Bicolor damselfish
entities.fact: The bicolor damselfish chirps and pops at intruders on Caribbean reefs, and its calls were among the first fish sounds studied in detail.

entities.name: Danionella cerebrum
entities.fact: Danionella cerebrum, a transparent fish 12 millimetres long from Myanmar, makes sounds of over 140 decibels by flicking a piece of cartilage against its swim bladder.

entities.name: Gar
entities.fact: Gars are armoured, needle-nosed fish of North American rivers that gulp air at the surface and leap when hooked, and the alligator gar can reach 3 metres.

entities.name: Needlefish
entities.fact: Needlefish have long beak-like jaws full of teeth and skim the surface at speed, occasionally spearing boaters when they leap.

entities.name: Sawshark
entities.fact: Sawsharks carry a long flat saw-like snout with a pair of trailing barbels, and unlike sawfish they have gills on the sides of the head.

entities.name: Unicornfish
entities.fact: Unicornfish are surgeonfish with a horn-like projection on the forehead, and they carry sharp blades at the base of the tail.

entities.name: Elephantnose fish
entities.fact: Peters's elephantnose fish of African rivers has a finger-like chin extension packed with electric sensors, used to probe the mud for food.

entities.name: Longnose butterflyfish
entities.fact: The longnose butterflyfish uses its long thin snout like tweezers to pluck tiny animals from coral crevices, and is yellow with a black eye mask.

entities.name: Halfbeak
entities.fact: Halfbeaks have a long lower jaw and a short upper one, and they skim the surface eating floating seaweed and small animals.

entities.name: Cornetfish
entities.fact: The cornetfish is an extremely slender reef fish up to 1.5 metres long, with a tubular snout and a whip-like filament trailing from its tail.

entities.name: Shovelnose guitarfish
entities.fact: The shovelnose guitarfish is a ray with a pointed shovel-shaped snout and a shark-like tail, lying on sandy bottoms off California and Mexico.

entities.name: Longnose hawkfish
entities.fact: The longnose hawkfish perches on deep gorgonian sea fans wearing a red check pattern, with a long snout for plucking tiny shrimps.

entities.name: Snipefish
entities.fact: The snipefish is a small deep-water relative of seahorses with a long tube snout, named after the wading bird with a long bill.

entities.name: Long-nosed chimaera
entities.fact: Long-nosed chimaeras are deep-sea ghost sharks with a long pointed snout covered in electric-sensing pores.

entities.name: Longnose skate
entities.fact: The longnose skate of the North American Pacific coast has a long pointed snout and lays eggs in leathery cases known as mermaid's purses.

entities.name: Shrimpfish
entities.fact: Shrimpfish, or razorfish, are thin armoured relatives of seahorses that swim head-down in synchronised groups, often hiding among sea urchin spines.

entities.name: Seamoth
entities.fact: Seamoths are small armoured fish with wing-like fins and a long flat snout, and they walk across the sand on their pelvic fins.

entities.name: Longnose batfish
entities.fact: The longnose batfish walks across the seabed on arm-like fins, has a pointed snout, and dangles a tiny lure from beneath it to attract prey.

entities.name: Slender snipe eel
entities.fact: The slender snipe eel has bird-like jaws so long and thin that they curve apart and cannot close, and its body reaches 1.5 metres but is only as thick as a finger.

entities.name: Trout
entities.fact: Trout leap clear of the water to snatch insects and to climb small waterfalls on the way upstream to spawn.

entities.name: Silver carp
entities.fact: Silver carp, invasive in US rivers, leap up to 3 metres into the air when startled by boat motors, injuring boaters.

entities.name: Spinner shark
entities.fact: The spinner shark charges up through schools of fish and bursts from the surface spinning on its axis, landing with a splash.

entities.name: Spotted eagle ray
entities.fact: Spotted eagle rays leap clear of the water, sometimes several times in a row, and have been known to land in boats.

entities.name: Thresher shark
entities.fact: Thresher sharks breach fully out of the water and stun fish with their enormous scythe-like tails, which make up half their length.

entities.name: Mobula ray
entities.fact: Mobula rays, or devil rays, gather in schools of thousands off Mexico and leap metres into the air, flipping and belly-flopping back down.

entities.name: Barracuda
entities.fact: Great barracuda leap out of the water when hooked, strike at speeds of around 40 kilometres per hour, and have a reputation for following divers.

entities.name: Ladyfish
entities.fact: The ladyfish is a slim silver fish of warm estuaries that leaps and skips repeatedly across the surface when hooked.

entities.name: Northern pike
entities.fact: Northern pike lunge at prey from cover and leap clear of the water when hooked, and they can reach well over a metre long.

entities.name: Houndfish
entities.fact: The houndfish is a 1.5-metre needlefish that leaps from the water at speed and has impaled fishermen with its beak.

entities.name: African tigerfish
entities.fact: The African tigerfish has been filmed leaping from the water to snatch swallows out of the air, the first freshwater fish confirmed to catch birds in flight.

entities.name: Pacific leaping blenny
entities.fact: The Pacific leaping blenny of Guam lives entirely out of water on wave-splashed rocks, leaping between them by curling and flicking its tail.
